question.text: Which of the following statements regarding electroencephalogram (EEG) is not correct?

options.label: A
options.text: 1-5% of the population can have epileptiform discharges

options.label: B
options.text: Doing EEG is mandatory for diagnosis of seizures

options.label: C
options.text: Scalp EEG may be helpful in localizing frontal lobe epilepsy

options.label: D
options.text: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy shows triphasic and slow waves on EEG AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (B) Doing EEG is mandatory for diagnosis of seizures This statement is not correct. The diagnosis of epilepsy and seizures is primarily a clinical diagnosis, based on a thorough history and eyewitness accounts of the events. An electroencephalogram (EEG) is a crucial investigative tool that provides supportive evidence. It can help classify the seizure type, identify an epileptogenic focus, and guide treatment, but it is not mandatory for diagnosis. A patient can have a definitive clinical diagnosis of epilepsy even if their interictal (between seizures) EEG is normal. Conversely, a small percentage of the healthy population (A) can have incidental epileptiform discharges on their EEG without ever having a seizure. EEG is helpful in localizing certain epilepsies (C), and various encephalopathies can show specific patterns like slow or triphasic waves (D). But the diagnosis of a seizure remains fundamentally clinical. 129. Which jugular venous pressure (JVP) wave corresponds to the isovolumetric contraction phase of the cardiac cycle? (A) A wave (B) C wave (C) X descent (D) Y descent AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (B) C wave The jugular venous pressure (JVP) waveform reflects pressure changes in the right atrium. The 'a' wave (A) is caused by atrial contraction. The 'c' wave is a small positive wave that occurs during early ventricular systole. It is thought to be caused by the bulging of the tricuspid valve back into the right atrium as it closes at the beginning of isovolumetric ventricular contraction. It can also have a component from the transmitted carotid artery pulsation. The 'x' descent (C) is the fall in atrial pressure caused by atrial relaxation and the downward pulling of the tricuspid valve during ventricular systole. The 'v' wave is caused by atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve. The 'y' descent (D) is the fall in atrial pressure when the tricuspid valve opens and the ventricle begins to fill. Therefore, the c wave corresponds to the isovolumetric contraction phase. 130. A 22-year-old male arrives at the emergency department after a car accident. His Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is E2M2V3. There are no fractures, no signs of hydrocephalus or raised intracranial pressure, and his non-contrast CT scan is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis? (A) Diffuse axonal injury (B) Post-concussion syndrome (C) Extradural hemorrhage (D) Herniation of brain AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (A) Diffuse axonal injury The patient has a severe traumatic brain injury, as indicated by his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score. The total score is E2 (opens eyes to pain) + M2 (extends to pain) + V3 (inappropriate words) = 7. A GCS of 3-8 defines a severe TBI. The key feature of the case is the profound neurological impairment in the face of a normal initial non-contrast CT scan. This discrepancy is the hallmark of diffuse axonal injury (DAI). DAI is caused by shearing forces from the trauma that lead to widespread microscopic damage to axons, which is not visible on a standard CT scan. Macroscopic injuries like an extradural hemorrhage (C) or signs of herniation (D) would be readily apparent on CT. Post-concussion syndrome (B) describes persistent symptoms after a mild TBI, which is inconsistent with a GCS of 7. 131. What is the mechanism by which the toxin causing the abdominal posturing shown in the image produces generalized muscle spasms and back arching in a 45-year-old man who recently sustained a puncture wound to his leg? (A) Presynaptic inhibitor of GABA and glycine release (B) Presynaptic inhibitor of Ach receptors (C) Postsynaptic inhibitor of GABA (D) Cleavage of SNARE proteins preventing Ach release AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (A) Presynaptic inhibitor of GABA and glycine release The clinical presentation of generalized muscle spasms, opisthotonus (arching of the back), and risus sardonicus following a puncture wound is diagnostic of tetanus. The disease is caused by the potent neurotoxin, tetanospasmin, produced by the bacterium Clostridium tetani. The toxin travels retrograde up motor neurons to the central nervous system. In the spinal cord, it acts on inhibitory interneurons (Renshaw cells). The toxin is a zinc-dependent endopeptidase that cleaves a protein called synaptobrevin (a SNARE protein), which is essential for the fusion of neurotransmitter vesicles with the presynaptic membrane. By doing so, it blocks the presynaptic release of inhibitory neurotransmitters, primarily glycine and GABA. This loss of inhibition leads to the unregulated firing of alpha motor neurons, causing simultaneous contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles, resulting in the characteristic rigid paralysis and spasms. SURGERY 132. A 26-year-old man presents with a large, painless, firm swelling in the right testicle and a dragging sensation. The left testicle is normal, and his AFP level is around 3000 U. What is the most appropriate next step in management? (A) FNAC (Fine needle aspiration cytology) (B) Scrotal trucut biopsy (C) High inguinal orchidectomy (D) Repeat tumor markers AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (C) High inguinal orchidectomy A painless, firm testicular mass in a young man is considered a testicular cancer until proven otherwise. The markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level confirms the presence of a non-seminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT), as seminomas do not produce AFP. The standard and essential next step in management is a radical high inguinal orchidectomy. This procedure involves removing the entire testicle and spermatic cord through an incision in the groin. It is both diagnostic (providing the entire specimen for histology) and therapeutic (removing the primary tumor). A trans-scrotal approach, such as an FNAC (A) or trucut biopsy (B), is absolutely contraindicated. This is because it violates the scrotal lymphatic drainage, which is distinct from the testicular lymphatic drainage (to the retroperitoneal nodes), and can lead to scrotal seeding and altered patterns of metastasis, complicating subsequent treatment. 133. What is the most frequent reason for hospital admission following daycare surgery? (A) Postoperative nausea and vomiting (B) Respiratory distress (C) Post-surgical pain (D) Bleeding AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (A) Postoperative nausea and vomiting Daycare surgery, or ambulatory surgery, relies on the patient being able to recover safely and comfortably at home. One of the most common and distressing side effects that can prevent a timely discharge or lead to an unplanned hospital admission is intractable postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). While post-surgical pain (C) is also very common, it can often be managed with oral analgesics. However, persistent nausea and vomiting can lead to dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, and an inability to tolerate oral fluids or medications, necessitating admission for intravenous hydration and antiemetic therapy. answer.correctText: Doing EEG is mandatory for diagnosis of seizures
answer.explanation: seizures This statement is not correct. The diagnosis of epilepsy and seizures is primarily a clinical diagnosis, based on a thorough history and eyewitness accounts of the events. An electroencephalogram (EEG) is a crucial investigative tool that provides supportive evidence. It can help classify the seizure type, identify an epileptogenic focus, and guide treatment, but it is not mandatory for diagnosis. A patient can have a definitive clinical diagnosis of epilepsy even if their interictal (between seizures) EEG is normal. Conversely, a small percentage of the healthy population (A) can have incidental epileptiform discharges on their EEG without ever having a seizure. EEG is helpful in localizing certain epilepsies (C), and various encephalopathies can show specific patterns like slow or triphasic waves (D). options.text: To confirm definitive diagnosis immediately in all cases AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (D) To confirm definitive diagnosis immediately in all cases Frozen section is an invaluable intraoperative tool. It allows for rapid microscopic analysis of a tissue sample while the patient is still under anesthesia. It is routinely used to determine the status of the sentinel lymph node (A), which helps guide the decision on whether to proceed with an axillary lymph node dissection. It is also used to assess surgical margins (B) to ensure the tumor has been completely excised. It can also identify unexpected metastasis (C). However, its major limitation is that the tissue quality is inferior to that of permanent, formalin-fixed sections. For certain challenging cases, such as differentiating ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) from atypical ductal hyperplasia, or in some types of lobular carcinoma, a frozen section may not be able to provide a definitive diagnosis immediately in all cases (D). In such situations, the pathologist will defer the final diagnosis to the permanent sections. 139. The following drain is placed after a mastectomy. Identify the type of drain shown in the image. (A) Open (B) Closed (C) Semi open (D) Semi closed AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (B) Closed The image shows a Jackson-Pratt (JP) drain. This is a type of closed suction drain. It consists of a perforated tube that is placed in the surgical wound, connected via tubing to a compressible, bulb-shaped reservoir. After placement, the bulb is squeezed to remove the air, creating a vacuum or negative pressure. This gentle, constant suction pulls excess fluid, blood, and serous drainage from the wound into the bulb, preventing the formation of a hematoma or seroma and promoting healing. It is a "closed" system because the drainage pathway is entirely contained, from the patient to the collection bulb, which minimizes the risk of retrograde bacterial contamination of the wound. An open drain, like a Penrose drain, simply allows fluid to drain onto a dressing. 140. Which of the following statements about hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is/are correct? 1. TACE is used for multinodular lesions Click Here to Buy book on Amazon MEDINK EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 2. Lenvatinib is used for lesions less than 3 cm 3. The incidence of HCC is increasing 4. NASH and NAFLD are risk factors for HCC (TACE : Transarterial chemoembolization) (A) 1,2,3 (B) 2,3,4 (C) 1,3,4 (D) 1 and 2 AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (C) 1,3,4 1. Correct. Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) is a primary treatment modality for patients with intermediate-stage HCC, which is typically defined as large or multinodular tumors confined to the liver, in patients with preserved liver function who are not candidates for curative therapies. 2. Incorrect. Lenvatinib is a systemic tyrosine kinase inhibitor used to treat advanced or unresectable HCC, not small, early-stage lesions. Lesions less than 3 cm would be candidates for curative treatments like resection, ablation, or transplantation. 3. Correct. The global incidence of HCC is increasing, largely driven by the rising prevalence of its risk factors, particularly Hepatitis C, and now increasingly, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. 4. Correct. While chronic viral hepatitis (B and C) and alcoholic liver disease are the most common risk factors worldwide, Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and its inflammatory form, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), are rapidly emerging as leading causes of cirrhosis and subsequent HCC, especially in Western countries. 141. A patient arrives at the emergency department after a road traffic accident with a 4 × 1 cm bone-deep lacerated wound on the scalp of the forehead. What is the most likely mechanism responsible for this type of laceration? (A) Shearing force (B) Impact of a semi-sharp edged object (C) Overstretching of skin and subcutaneous tissue (D) Tissue crushed between weapon and underlying bone AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (D) Tissue crushed between weapon and underlying bone A laceration is a tear or split in the skin and underlying tissues caused by blunt force trauma, as opposed to an incised wound from a sharp object. On the scalp and forehead, the skin is relatively thin and stretched tautly over the underlying rigid skull. When a blunt object impacts this area, the soft tissue is momentarily and forcefully compressed and crushed between the impacting object and the underlying bone. This crushing force exceeds the elastic capacity of the skin, causing it to split open, creating a laceration. These lacerations often have irregular, bruised edges and may have "tissue bridges" of intact nerves or vessels crossing the wound depths, which are characteristic of a blunt force mechanism. 142. In the para-sagittal abdominal section shown, what forms the upper boundary of the highlighted structure? (A) Caudate lobe of liver (B) Duodenum (C) Lesser omentum (D) Inferior vena cava AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (A) Caudate lobe of liver The image shows a sagittal view of the upper abdomen with the lesser sac (omental bursa) highlighted. The lesser sac is a potential space in the abdominal cavity, located posterior to the stomach and lesser omentum. It is important to know its anatomical boundaries. The superior boundary, or roof, of the lesser sac is formed by the visceral peritoneum covering the caudate lobe of the liver. The anterior boundary is the stomach, lesser omentum, and gastrocolic ligament. The posterior boundary is the pancreas and peritoneum covering the posterior abdominal wall structures. The inferior boundary is the transverse mesocolon. The entrance to the lesser sac is the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow), whose superior boundary is also the caudate lobe. PEDIATRICS 143. What is the primary reason for bladder outlet obstruction in male children? (A) Posterior urethral valve (B) Urethral atresia (C) Anterior urethral valve (D) Ureterocele AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (A) Posterior urethral valve The most common cause of significant bladder outlet obstruction in male infants and children is the presence of posterior urethral valves (PUV). PUV is a congenital condition where obstructing leaflets or membranes of tissue are present in the posterior (prostatic) urethra. These valves act as a one-way flap, impeding the outflow of urine from the bladder. This obstruction can be severe, leading to high pressure within the bladder, bilateral hydroureteronephrosis (dilation of the ureters and kidneys), and progressive renal damage, even in utero. It is a serious condition that requires prompt diagnosis and surgical intervention (valve ablation). Anterior urethral valves (C) are much rarer. Urethral atresia (B) is incompatible with life unless a urinary diversion is present. A ureterocele (D) can cause obstruction but typically at the ureterovesical junction. 144. Which organism is most likely responsible for infection in a 14-day-old neonate presenting with bilateral conjunctivitis and lung infiltrates on chest X-ray? (A) Chlamydia trachomatis (B) Haemophilus influenzae (C) Streptococcus (D) Mycoplasma AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (A) Chlamydia trachomatis The combination of conjunctivitis and pneumonia in a neonate between 1 to 3 weeks of age is the classic presentation of a perinatal infection with Chlamydia trachomatis. The infant acquires the infection during passage through an infected birth canal. The conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) typically appears 5 to 14 days after birth and is characterized by a watery to mucopurulent discharge. This is often followed by the development of a distinctive afebrile pneumonia, characterized by a staccato cough, tachypnea, and diffuse interstitial infiltrates on the chest X-ray. This specific constellation of delayed-onset conjunctivitis and afebrile pneumonia is highly characteristic of neonatal chlamydial infection. The other organisms listed cause neonatal infections but are not typically associated with this specific combined syndrome. 145. Which of the following components make up kangaroo mother care? (A) Early discharge, skin-to-skin contact, prevent infection (B) Early discharge, skin-to-skin contact, exclusive breastfeeding (C) Skin-to-skin contact, exclusive breastfeeding, prevent infection (D) Early discharge, exclusive breastfeeding and prevent infection AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (B) Early discharge, skin-to-skin contact, exclusive breastfeeding Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) is a comprehensive, low-cost intervention for the care of low-birth-weight and preterm infants, particularl

question.text: A patient arrives at the emergency department after a road traffic accident with a 4 × 1 cm bone-deep lacerated wound on the scalp of the forehead. What is the most likely mechanism responsible for this type of laceration?

options.label: B

options.text: Tissue crushed between weapon and underlying bone AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (D) Tissue crushed between weapon and underlying bone A laceration is a tear or split in the skin and underlying tissues caused by blunt force trauma, as opposed to an incised wound from a sharp object. answer.explanation: The most common cause of significant bladder outlet obstruction in male infants and children is the presence of posterior urethral valves (PUV). PUV is a congenital condition where obstructing leaflets or membranes of tissue are present in the posterior (prostatic) urethra. These valves act as a one-way flap, impeding the outflow of urine from the bladder. This obstruction can be severe, leading to high pressure within the bladder, bilateral hydroureteronephrosis (dilation of the ureters and kidneys), and progressive renal damage, even in utero. It is a serious condition that requires prompt diagnosis and surgical intervention (valve ablation). Anterior urethral valves (C) are much rarer. Urethral atresia (B) is incompatible with life unless a urinary diversion is present. A ureterocele (D) can cause obstruction but typically at the ureterovesical junction. options.text: Haemophilus produces beta-lactamase, hence resistant to ampicillin AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (D) Hemophilus produces beta-lactamase, hence resistant to ampicillin The most common mechanism of resistance to ampicillin in Hemophilus influenzae is the production of the enzyme beta-lactamase. This enzyme hydrolyzes the beta-lactam ring of penicillin-class antibiotics like ampicillin, inactivating the drug. A significant proportion of H. influenzae strains, including those causing invasive diseases like meningitis, are beta-lactamase positive. For this reason, ampicillin is no longer recommended as a sole empirical therapy for serious H. influenzae infections. Third-generation cephalosporins, such as ceftriaxone, are stable in the presence of these beta-lactamases and have excellent penetration into the cerebrospinal fluid, making them the drug of choice for treating H. influenzae meningitis. A 32-year-old pregnant woman with monochorionic diamniotic twins shows polyhydramnios in one twin and oligohydramnios in the other on an ultrasound. This serious complication arises due to unbalanced blood flow through inter-twin vascular anastomoses on the shared placental surface. One twin, the "donor," transfuses blood to the other, the "recipient." The donor twin becomes anemic and hypovolemic, leading to poor renal perfusion and oligohydramnios. The recipient twin becomes hypervolemic and polycythemic, leading to cardiac strain and polyuria, which results in polyhydramnios. This combination of oligohydramnios in the donor and polyhydramnios in the recipient is the defining feature of TTTS. 169. answer.explanation: This question tests the knowledge of eponymous fractures of the hand and foot. A Jones fracture (a) is a specific transverse fracture of the proximal 5th metatarsal bone of the foot, occurring at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction. A Bennett's fracture (b) is an intra-articular fracture involving the base of the 1st metacarpal bone in the hand, resulting in a fracture-dislocation of the carpometacarpal joint. A March fracture (c) is a type of stress fracture affecting the metatarsal bones of the foot, most commonly the neck of the 2nd metatarsal, and is typically seen in soldiers or athletes due to repetitive stress. A Boxer fracture (d) is a fracture of the neck of a metacarpal bone, most frequently the 5th metacarpal, which is commonly sustained by punching a hard object with a closed fist. question.text: Please match the following fractures with their corresponding locations. a. Jones fracture 1. 5th metatarsal b. Bennett's fracture 2. 2nd metatarsal c. March fracture 3. 1st metacarpal d. Boxer fracture 4. 5th metacarpal

options.label: D
options.text: a-2, b-4, c-1, d-3 AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (A) a-1, b-3, c-2, d-4 This is a duplicate of the previous question. To reiterate the definitions, these fractures have specific anatomical locations. The Jones fracture (a) specifically affects the proximal 5th metatarsal (1). The Bennett's fracture (b) is an oblique, intra-articular fracture occurring at the base of the 1st metacarpal (3). The March fracture (c) is a fatigue fracture, most often seen in the shaft of the 2nd metatarsal (2), caused by repetitive stress from activities like prolonged walking or running. Lastly, the Boxer fracture (d) is a common injury resulting from a direct blow with a clenched fist, causing a fracture at the neck of the 5th metacarpal (4). Correctly pairing these eponymous fractures with their respective bones yields the combination a-1, b-3, c-2, d-4, confirming the correct answer choice. 153. Arrange the steps for performing the Thomas Test—used to evaluate a hip flexion deformity— in the correct order. 1. Squaring of the pelvis 2. Flexion of the hip 3. Look for exaggerated lumbar lordosis 4. Measure the actual flexion deformity 5. Ensure the ischial tuberosity makes contact with the ground 6. Overcorrect the normal side (A) 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (B) 3, 2, 1, 4, 6 (C) 3, 2, 6, 5, 4 (D) 3, 6, 2, 5, 4 AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (C) 3, 2, 6, 5, 4 The Thomas test is used to assess fixed flexion deformity of the hip. Correct sequence: 3. Look for exaggerated lumbar lordosis : The patient lies supine. First observe for increased lumbar lordosis, which suggests a possible hip flexion deformity. 2. Flexion of the hip : Flex the normal (unaffected) hip to flatten the lumbar spine and eliminate lumbar lordosis. 6. Overcorrect the normal side : Further flex the normal hip until the pelvis begins to rotate, ensuring complete correction of pelvic tilt. 5. Ensure the ischial tuberosity makes contact with the ground : Confirm that the pelvis is stabilized and the lumbar spine is flat against the table (pelvis “squared”). 4. Measure the actual flexion deformity : The angle between the affected thigh and the table is then measured—this represents the fixed flexion deformity. Thus, the correct order is : 3 → 2 → 6 → 5 → 4, which corresponds to Option (C). 154. A 60-year-old woman with a Colles’ fracture 8 months ago, a T-score of –2.5, menopause at age 52, and no current symptoms attends the orthopedics clinic. What is the most appropriate treatment for her? (A) Hormone replacement therapy (B) Alendronate (C) Calcium and vitamin D (D) Repeat DEXA scan after 3 months AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (B) Alendronate This patient has a definitive diagnosis of severe osteoporosis and is at high risk for future fractures. The diagnosis is established by two key findings : first, a DEXA scan T-score of -2.5 or lower is the densitometric definition of osteoporosis. Second, she has already sustained a fragility fracture (a Colles' fracture from a low-impact fall), which is a clinical diagnosis of severe osteoporosis regardless of the T-score. Given her high risk, pharmacological intervention is mandatory. The first-line treatment for postmenopausal osteoporosis is a bisphosphonate, such as alendronate. These drugs are anti-resorptive agents that inhibit osteoclast activity, increase bone mineral density, and have been proven to significantly reduce the risk of vertebral and non-vertebral fractures. While calcium and vitamin D supplementation (C) is essential for all patients with osteoporosis, it is not sufficient as a standalone treatment. Repeating the DEXA scan (D) would unnecessarily delay essential treatment. Hormone replacement therapy (A) is not a first-line option. 155. A 45-year-old patient comes to the emergency department with severe pain in a casted tibial fracture. After the cast is removed, examination reveals painful passive extension, intact dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, and loss of sensation over the first web space. What is the most appropriate next step in management? (A) Duplex imaging (B) Re-apply cast (C) Measure anterior compartment pressure (D) Analgesics AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (C) Measure anterior compartment pressure This patient's clinical presentation is highly suggestive of acute compartment syndrome of the leg, an orthopedic emergency. The "5 P's" are classic, but the most reliable and earliest signs are present here : Pain out of proportion to the injury, which is not relieved by analgesics, and Pain on passive stretch of the muscles in the affected compartment. The sensory loss in the first web space indicates compression of the deep peroneal nerve, which runs through the anterior compartment. This Paresthesia is another key early sign. Pulses often remain intact until very late, so their presence is not reassuring. The most critical and urgent next step is to objectively confirm the diagnosis by measuring the intracompartmental pressure of the anterior compartment using a pressure monitor. A pressure reading within 30 mmHg of the diastolic blood pressure is highly indicative of compartment syndrome and necessitates an emergency surgical fasciotomy to prevent irreversible muscle and nerve damage. Duplex imaging (A) would rule out vascular injury but not compartment syndrome. 156. Match each bone condition with its most appropriate treatment : 1. Osteosarcoma a. Wide excision 2. Simple bone cyst b. Curettage 3. Giant cell tu- mor c. Radiofrequency ab- lation 4. Osteoid osteo- ma d. Intralesional steroid (A) 1-d, 2-c, 3-b, 4-a (B) 1-c, 2-a, 3-d. 4-b (C) 1-a, 2-d, 3-b, 4-c (D) 1-d, 2-a, 3-b, 4-c AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (C) 1-a, 2-d, 3-b, 4-c The matching requires knowledge of standard treatments for various bone tumors. Osteosarcoma (1) is a highly malignant primary bone cancer. The standard of care involves neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by limb-sparing surgery, which requires wide excision (a) of the tumor with clear margins to prevent local recurrence. A simple bone cyst (2) is a benign, fluid-filled lesion common in children. A standard, minimally invasive treatment is aspiration of the cyst fluid followed by intralesional steroid injection (d) to promote healing. A giant cell tumor (3) of bone is a benign but locally aggressive tumor. The most common treatment is meticulous curettage (b), where the tumor is scraped out from the bone, often combined with an adjuvant like phenol or cryotherapy to kill any remaining cells. An osteoid osteoma (4) is a small, benign tumor causing classic night pain. The modern treatment of choice is minimally invasive percutaneous radiofrequency ablation (c), which uses heat to destroy the tumor's nidus. 157. answer.explanation: This is a duplicate of a previous question. The clinical findings are classic for acute compartment syndrome. The severe pain, especially pain on passive stretch of the toe extensors, is the most sensitive early sign. The loss of sensation in the first web space indicates dysfunction of the deep peroneal nerve, which lies in the anterior compartment, and is another critical finding. The presence of distal pulses is not a reliable sign to rule out compartment syndrome, as pulses are often lost only in the late stages. The immediate and most appropriate next action is to confirm the clinical suspicion by objectively measuring the pressure within the anterior compartment. A high pressure confirms the diagnosis and mandates an emergency fasciotomy to prevent irreversible ischemic damage to the muscles and nerves within the compartment. Delaying diagnosis by pursuing other investigations or providing only analgesics can lead to devastating consequences, including limb loss. options.text: D AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (C) C The patient has difficulty flexing the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of the 4th and 5th fingers and cannot hold a piece of paper between the fingers. This suggests ulnar nerve injury. Ulnar nerve supplies: 1. Flexor digitorum profundus (medial half) → flexion of DIP joints of 4th and 5th digits 2. Interossei muscles → responsible for finger adduction (holding paper between fingers) 3. Lumbricals (medial two) Loss of DIP flexion in the 4th and 5th digits indicates involvement proximal to the branch supplying flexor digitorum profundus (i.e., above the wrist). In the image, point C corresponds to the medial epicondyle of the humerus, where the ulnar nerve passes posteriorly in the cubital tunnel. This is a common site of injury (“funny bone”). What nerve injury is responsible for the hand deformity shown in the image? (A) Ulnar nerve (B) Radial nerve (C) Median nerve (D) Posterior interosseous nerve AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (A) Ulnar nerve The image displays a classic claw hand deformity, specifically an ulnar claw hand, affecting the 4th and 5th digits. This deformity is caused by an injury to the ulnar nerve. The ulnar nerve innervates the medial two lumbricals (for the 4th and 5th fingers) and all of the interosseous muscles. The lumbricals are responsible for flexing the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints while extending the interphalangeal (IP) joints. When these intrinsic muscles are paralyzed, their actions are lost. The unopposed action of the long extensor muscles (innervated by the radial nerve) causes hyperextension at the MCP joints. Simultaneously, the unopposed action of the flexor digitorum profundus (partially innervated by the median nerve for these fingers in some cases, but the functional loss is key) causes flexion at the IP joints. This combination of MCP hyperextension and IP flexion creates the characteristic "claw" appearance of the affected fingers. OBS & GYNE 161. Which of the following is not considered a lower urinary tract symptom (LUTS)? (A) Sudden urge to urinate (B) Incontinence while asleep (C) Incontinence when patient lies down and coughs (D) Incontinence during intercourse AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (D) Incontinence during intercourse Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) refer to symptoms arising from the bladder, urethra, or prostate and are classified into storage, voiding, and post-micturition symptoms. Storage symptoms include urgency, frequency, nocturia, and urinary incontinence. 1. Option (A), sudden urge to urinate, represents urgency and is a classic storage symptom of LUTS. 2. Option (B), incontinence while asleep, corresponds to nocturnal enuresis and is also categorized under storage LUTS. 3. Option (C), incontinence when the patient lies down and coughs, describes stress urinary incontinence, which occurs due to increased intra-abdominal pressure and is included among lower urinary tract symptoms. 4. Option (D), incontinence during intercourse, is termed coital incontinence. Although it involves urinary leakage, it is generally considered part of sexual dysfunction rather than being classified within the standard LUTS framework. It is not routinely included in the International Continence Society’s core LUTS classification. Therefore, the correct answer is (D) Incontinence during intercourse. 162. Based on the provided clinical image, what would be the most likely diagnosis? (A) Cervical carcinoma (B) Uterine inversion (C) Uterocervical prolapse (D) Fibroid polyp AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (C) Uterocervical prolapse Uterocervical prolapse refers to the descent of the uterus and cervix through the vaginal canal due to weakness of the pelvic floor muscles and supporting ligaments such as the uterosacral and cardinal ligaments. It is commonly seen in multiparous, postmenopausal women and may present with a mass protruding per vaginum, pelvic pressure, backache, and urinary symptoms. In a typical clinical image of uterocervical prolapse, a rounded mass is seen protruding from the vaginal introitus. The cervix may be visible at the most dependent part of the prolapsed mass, and in advanced stages, the entire uterus may descend outside the vaginal opening. Cervical carcinoma usually presents as an irregular, ulcerative, friable growth on the cervix rather than a smooth descending mass. Uterine inversion typically occurs postpartum and presents as a sudden collapse with a fundal mass. A fibroid polyp appears as a localized pedunculated mass rather than complete uterine descent. Thus, the most likely diagnosis is uterocervical prolapse. 163. A 26-year-old woman with two previous vaginal deliveries presents with ongoing abdominal discomfort, irregular menstrual cycles, and a palpable mass on vaginal examination. Ultrasound confirms a 5 × 5 cm ovarian cyst. What is the most appropriate next step in her management? (A) Follow up after 6 weeks (B) Measure CA 125 levels (C) Laparoscopy (D) CT pelvis AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (A) Follow up after 6 weeks The management of an ovarian cyst in a premenopausal woman depends on its size, characteristics on ultrasound, and the presence of symptoms. In this 26-year-old patient, a 5x5 cm cyst is discovered. The vast majority of such cysts in this age group are benign, functional cysts (e.g., follicular or corpus luteum cysts) that are related to the menstrual cycle. The standard and most appropriate initial management for a simple-appearing cyst of this size in a premenopausal woman is conservative. This involves a period of observation with a follow-up ultrasound after 6-8 weeks, which covers one to two menstrual cycles. Most functional cysts will resolve spontaneously within this time frame. Measuring CA 125 (B) is generally not recommended as a first step in premenopausal women as it can be elevated by many benign conditions. Immediate surgical intervention like laparoscopy (C) or further imaging with a CT scan (D) is not indicated unless the cyst has suspicious features (e.g., solid components, septations) or is causing acute symptoms like torsion. answer.explanation: The image displays a classic claw hand deformity, specifically an ulnar claw hand, affecting the 4th and 5th digits. This deformity is caused by an injury to the ulnar nerve. The ulnar nerve innervates the medial two lumbricals (for the 4th and 5th fingers) and all of the interosseous muscles. The lumbricals are responsible for flexing the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints while extending the interphalangeal (IP) joints. When these intrinsic muscles are paralyzed, their actions are lost. The unopposed action of the long extensor muscles (innervated by the radial nerve) causes hyperextension at the MCP joints. Simultaneously, the unopposed action of the flexor digitorum profundus (partially innervated by the median nerve for these fingers in some cases, but the functional loss is key) causes flexion at the IP joints. This combination of MCP hyperextension and IP flexion creates the characteristic "claw" appearance of the affected fingers. answer.explanation: Uterocervical prolapse refers to the descent of the uterus and cervix through the vaginal canal due to weakness of the pelvic floor muscles and supporting ligaments such as the uterosacral and cardinal ligaments. It is commonly seen in multiparous, postmenopausal women and may present with a mass protruding per vaginum, pelvic pressure, backache, and urinary symptoms. In a typical clinical image of uterocervical prolapse, a rounded mass is seen protruding from the vaginal introitus. The cervix may be visible at the most dependent part of the prolapsed mass, and in advanced stages, the entire uterus may descend outside the vaginal opening. Cervical carcinoma usually presents as an irregular, ulcerative, friable growth on the cervix rather than a smooth descending mass. Uterine inversion typically occurs postpartum and presents as a sudden collapse with a fundal mass. A fibroid polyp appears as a localized pedunculated mass rather than complete uterine descent. Thus, the most likely diagnosis is uterocervical prolapse. The test measures the levels of four specific substances in the mother's blood : 1. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) (C) 2. Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) (D) 3. Unconjugated estriol (uE3) (B) 4. Inhibin A These four markers are analyzed together with maternal age to calculate a risk score for Down syndrome (Trisomy 21), Trisomy 18, and open neural tube defects. Which fixative is employed for a Pap smear? (A) Formalin (B) Air dried (C) Normal saline (D) 95% ethanol AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (D) 95% ethanol For a conventional Papanicolaou (Pap) smear, proper and immediate fixation of the cervical cells on the glass slide is absolutely critical to preserve cellular morphology and prevent air-drying artifacts, which can render the specimen uninterpretable. The gold standard and most widely used fixative is 95% ethanol. The slide should be immersed in the ethanol solution or sprayed with a commercially available cytology spray fixative (which has an ethanol base) immediately after the sample is smeared. This wet-fixation process preserves the fine nuclear and cytoplasmic details necessary for accurate cytological diagnosis. Formalin (A) is the standard fixative for tissue biopsies (histology), not for cytology smears. Air drying (B) is used for hematology smears (e.g., peripheral blood) but causes significant distortion in Pap smears. Normal saline (C) is not a fixative. 166. What is considered the optimal percentage of normal sperm morphology in a semen analysis? (A) 10% (B) 4% (C) 6% (D) 8% AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (B) 4% According to the most recent World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for the examination and processing of human semen (5th and 6th editions), the lower reference limit for normal sperm morphology is 4%. This evaluation is performed using strict criteria, known as the Kruger's strict criteria, which assess the size and shape of the sperm head, midpiece, and tail. A semen sample is considered to have normal morphology if 4% or more of the observed spermatozoa have a normal form. A value below 4% is defined as teratozoospermia. This relatively low threshold reflects the high degree of morphological variability in human sperm and the stringent criteria used for classification. The older WHO editions used higher cut-off values, but the current standard is 4%. 167. What is the most likely diagnosis in an 18-year- old girl who has amenorrhea, normal genitalia and breast development, and tests positive for 5-alpha-reductase deficiency? (A) Mullerian agenesis (B) Concealed sex (C) AIS (Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome) (D) Turner's syndrome AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (B) Concealed sex. Let's break down the clinical picture to arrive at the diagnosis : 1. Patient Profile : An 18-year-old who appears female, with normal breast development and female external genitalia, but has never had a menstrual period (primary amenorrhea). 2. Key Lab Test : She tests positive for 5-alpha-reductase deficiency. 5-alpha-reductase is a crucial enzyme that converts testosterone into the much more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT). DHT is essential for the development of male external genitalia during fetal development. In an individual with a 46,XY (male) karyotype and 5-alpha-reductase deficiency : 1. In Utero : The lack of DHT means the external genitalia do not masculinize, leading to the development of female-appearing external genitalia. These individuals are typically assigned female at birth and raised as girls. 2. Internal Organs : They have testes (which may be undescended) that produce Anti-Müllerian Hormone, so they do not develop a uterus or fallopian tubes. This is why the patient has amenorrhea. 3. At Puberty : The testes produce a surge of testosterone. This testosterone can be converted into estrogen, leading to the development of female breasts. This entire scenario creates a discordance between the individual's genetic sex (male, XY) and their external physical appearance (female). This condition is what is being referred to by the somewhat outdated term "Concealed sex", as the male genetic identity is hidden by a female phenotype. Why Other Options Are Incorrect (A) Mullerian agenesis : This affects 46,XX (female) individuals who are born without a uterus. They have normal ovaries and develop breasts, but have amenorrhea. This diagnosis is inconsistent with a 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, which affects 46,XY individuals. (C) AIS (Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome) : This is also a condition in 46,XY individuals who appear female. However, the cause is a defect in androgen receptors, meaning their body cannot respond to testosterone or DHT. While the physical presentation is very similar, the specific diagnosis of 5-alpha-reductase deficiency rules out AIS. (D) Turner's syndrome : This is caused by a 45,X0 karyotype. These individuals are female but have non-functional ovaries, leading to a lack of estrogen and failure to develop breasts without hormone therapy. This does not match the patient's presentation. 168. A 32-year-old pregnant woman with monochorionic diamniotic twins shows polyhydramnios in one twin and oligohydramnios in the other on an ultrasound. What is the most likely complication indicated by these findings? (A) Selective fetal growth restriction (B) Preterm labor (C) Twin to twin transfusion syndrome (D) Neural tube defects AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (C) Twin to twin transfusion syndrome The ultrasound finding of polyhydramnios (excess amniotic fluid) in one twin and oligohydramnios (deficient amniotic fluid) in the other twin in a monochorionic pregnancy (twins sharing a single placenta) is the pathognomonic sign of Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS). One twin, the "donor," transfuses blood to the other, the "recipient." The donor twin becomes anemic and hypovolemic, leading to poor renal perfusion and oligohydramnios. The recipient twin becomes hypervolemic and polycythemic, leading to cardiac strain and polyuria, which results in polyhydramnios. This combination of oligohydramnios in the donor and polyhydramnios in the recipient is the defining feature of TTTS. 169. One twin, the "donor," transfuses blood to the other, the "recipient." The donor twin becomes anemic and hypovolemic, leading to poor renal perfusion and oligohydramnios. The recipient twin becomes hypervolemic and polycythemic, leading to cardiac strain and polyuria, which results in polyhydramnios. This combination of oligohydramnios in the donor and polyhydramnios in the recipient is the defining feature of TTTS. 169. What should be done for a newly diagnosed HIV patient who presents with fever, cough, and hemoptysis, and whose sputum sample shows acid-fast bacilli? According to WHO and other international guidelines, in patients with HIV and TB co-infection, treatment for tuberculosis must be prioritized. The recommended course of action is to start anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) immediately. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) should then be initiated shortly thereafter. The optimal timing is to start ART within 2 to 8 weeks of starting ATT. Starting ART too early, especially in patients with very low CD4 counts, can increase the risk of Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS), where a rapid recovery of the immune system can lead to a paradoxical worsening of the TB symptoms. A 68-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes, and coronary artery disease presents with palpitations and shortness of breath. His heartbeat is irregular, and ECG shows an irregular rhythm with no P waves and no isoelectric baseline. His vitals are BP 132/84 mmHg, HR 130 bpm, and SpO₂ 94% on room air. The heart rate of 130 bpm indicates a rapid ventricular response (RVR). Since the patient is hemodynamically stable (BP 132/84), the immediate goal of management is rate control, not rhythm control. The first-line agents for rate control in atrial fibrillation are either beta-blockers (like metoprolol) or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (like diltiazem). These drugs slow conduction through the AV node, thereby reducing the ventricular rate and improving symptoms. Electrical cardioversion (C) is reserved for unstable patients. Amiodarone (A) is typically a second-line agent for rate or rhythm control. Anticoagulation (D) is essential for long-term stroke prevention but is not the first-line intervention for acute rate control. 123. question.text: What is the fasting blood glucose cut-off value recommended by the IADPSG (International Association of Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Group) for the diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM)?

options.label: D
options.text: >90 mg/dL AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (A) >92 mg/dL The International Association of the Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups (IADPSG) proposed a one-step approach for diagnosing Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM), which has been adopted by many organizations, including the WHO and the American Diabetes Association. This approach involves a 75-gram, 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) performed between 24 and 28 weeks of gestation. GDM is diagnosed if any one of the following plasma glucose values is met or exceeded : 1. Fasting : ≥92 mg/dL 2. 1-hour : ≥180 mg/dL 3. 2-hour : ≥153 mg/dL Therefore, the specific IADPSG cut-off for the fasting blood glucose value is 92 mg/dL. The older two-step Carpenter-Coustan criteria used a fasting cut-off of >95 mg/dL (B). 173. What steps would you take to identify the cause of postmenopausal bleeding in a 62-year- old woman with a history of diabetes and hypertension? (A) Pap smear (B) Visual inspection with iodine (C) Colposcopy (D) Endometrial sampling AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (D) Endometrial sampling Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) is considered a cardinal sign of endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Any episode of vaginal bleeding occurring one year or more after menopause requires a thorough evaluation of the endometrium. The patient's risk factors for endometrial cancer are also significant (age, diabetes, hypertension). The most important and definitive step in the workup is to obtain a tissue sample from the uterine lining for histological analysis. This can be done via an office-based endometrial biopsy (a form of endometrial sampling) or a formal dilatation and curettage (D&C), often with hysteroscopy. A Pap smear (A) is a screening test for cervical cancer, not endometrial cancer, although it can occasionally detect endometrial cells. Visual inspection (B) and colposcopy (C) are used to evaluate the cervix, not the endometrium. 174. What does the World Health Organization (WHO) recommend for the management of the second stage of labor? (A) Mandatory episiotomy (B) Manual perineal support and warm compresses (C) Maintain head in deflexion and deliver (D) Deliver in lithotomy position only AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (B) Manual perineal support and warm compresses The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes a patient-centered, evidence-based approach to childbirth. For the management of the second stage of labor in a woman at low risk, the WHO recommends several practices to promote a positive birth experience and reduce trauma. These include encouraging the woman to push in a position of her choice and using techniques to protect the perineum. Specifically, the guidelines support the use of manual perineal support (guarding the perineum) and the application of warm compresses to the perineum during the second stage. These interventions have been shown to reduce the risk of third and fourth-degree perineal tears. The WHO explicitly recommends against routine or mandatory episiotomy (A). It also advises against maintaining the head in deflexion (C); flexion is the desired attitude. It encourages women to deliver in positions other than the lithotomy position (D). 175. Which diagnostic test is most effective for distinguishing obstructive azoospermia from testicular azoospermia in an infertile couple? (A) Serum FSH levels (B) Serum testosterone levels (C) Testicular biopsy (D) Serum LH levels AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (A) Serum FSH levels Azoospermia is the absence of sperm in the ejaculate. It can be caused by a blockage in the reproductive tract (obstructive azoospermia) or a failure of the testes to produce sperm (non-obstructive or testicular azoospermia). Measuring the serum Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) level is the most important initial blood test to differentiate between these two causes. The Sertoli cells in the testes produce inhibin B, which exerts negative feedback on pituitary FSH secretion. In non-obstructive azoospermia, the damaged testes fail to produce sperm and inhibin B, leading to a loss of negative feedback and consequently high serum FSH levels. In obstructive azoospermia, spermatogenesis is normal, so inhibin B levels are normal, and therefore FSH levels are also normal. Testosterone (B) and LH (D) levels can provide additional information but are less specific for differentiating the cause of azoospermia. 176. What is the prescribed dosage of dexamethasone administered to promote fetal lung maturity? (A) 2 doses of 6 mg given 12 hours apart (B) 2 doses of 12 mg given 24 hours apart (C) 4 doses of 6 mg given 12 hours apart (D) 4 doses of 12 mg given 12 hours apart AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (C) 4 doses of 6 mg given 12 hours apart Antenatal corticosteroids are administered to pregnant women at risk of preterm delivery to accelerate fetal lung maturation and reduce the risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. The two standard corticosteroid regimens are betamethasone and dexamethasone. The recommended regimen for dexamethasone consists of four intramuscular doses of 6 mg each, given 12 hours apart, for a total dose of 24 mg. The alternative regimen using betamethasone consists of two intramuscular doses of 12 mg each, given 24 hours apart (B), also for a total dose of 24 mg. Both regimens are considered equally effective. The question specifically asks for the dexamethasone dosage, which is 6 mg every 12 hours for a total of four doses. 177. Which emergency contraceptive is commonly utilized in India among the options provided? (A) Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg (B) Misoprostol 400 mcg (C) Ethinyl estradiol 600 mcg (D) Ulipristal 30 mg AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (A) Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg The most widely available and commonly used dedicated oral emergency contraceptive pill (ECP) in India, and indeed globally, is levonorgestrel. It is most effective when taken as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse. The standard regimen is a single dose of 1.5 mg. It is readily available over-the-counter in pharmacies under various brand names (e.g., i-Pill, Unwanted-72). Ulipristal acetate (D) is another effective oral ECP, but it is less commonly available in India and often requires a prescription. Misoprostol (B) is a prostaglandin analogue used for medical abortion and labor induction, not as an emergency contraceptive. High-dose ethinyl estradiol (C) was part of the older, less effective, and side-effect-prone Yuzpe regimen, which is no longer recommended. 178. What medication is recommended for treating foul-smelling vaginal discharge in a 24-year- old woman, based on the provided microscopic image? (A) Clindamycin (B) Cotrimoxazole (C) Azithromycin (D) Metronidazole AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (D) Metronidazole The microscopic image displays "clue cells," which are vaginal epithelial cells that are heavily coated with bacteria, giving them a stippled or granular appearance and obscuring the cell borders. The presence of clue cells on a saline wet mount is the most reliable diagnostic sign of bacterial vaginosis (BV). BV is a common cause of vaginal discharge, which is typically thin, grayish-white, and has a characteristic "fishy" odor, especially after intercourse. It is a polymicrobial condition involving an overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria. The first-line recommended treatment for bacterial vaginosis is the antibiotic metronidazole, which has excellent activity against a broad range of anaerobic bacteria. It can be administered either orally (e.g., 500 mg twice daily for 7 days) or as an intravaginal gel. Clindamycin (A) is an effective alternative treatment. 179. answer.explanation: Azoospermia is the absence of sperm in the ejaculate. It can be caused by a blockage in the reproductive tract (obstructive azoospermia) or a failure of the testes to produce sperm (non-obstructive or testicular azoospermia). Measuring the serum Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) level is the most important initial blood test to differentiate between these two causes. The Sertoli cells in the testes produce inhibin B, which exerts negative feedback on pituitary FSH secretion. In non- obstructive azoospermia, the damaged testes fail to produce sperm and inhibin B, leading to a loss of negative feedback and consequently high serum FSH levels. In obstructive azoospermia, spermatogenesis is normal, so inhibin B levels are normal, and therefore FSH levels are also normal. Testosterone (B) and LH (D) levels can provide additional information but are less specific for differentiating the cause of azoospermia. answer.explanation: The microscopic image displays "clue cells," which are vaginal epithelial cells that are heavily coated with bacteria, giving them a stippled or granular appearance and obscuring the cell borders. The presence of clue cells on a saline wet mount is the most reliable diagnostic sign of bacterial vaginosis (BV). The first- line recommended treatment for bacterial vaginosis is the antibiotic metronidazole, which has excellent activity against a broad range of anaerobic bacteria. It can be administered either orally (e.g., 500 mg twice daily for 7 days) or as an intravaginal gel. Clindamycin (A) is an effective alternative treatment. (A) Photosensitive skin rash (B) Nail bed capillary changes (C) Gottron's papules (D) Malar rash AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (C) Gottron's papules Juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM) is an autoimmune inflammatory disease affecting the skin and muscles. While it presents with a constellation of signs, certain skin findings are considered pathognomonic, meaning they are so characteristic that their presence is virtually diagnostic. The two pathognomonic signs of dermatomyositis are the heliotrope rash (a violaceous rash on the eyelids) and Gottron's papules. Gottron's papules are erythematous to violaceous, scaly papules and plaques located over the extensor surfaces of the joints, most classically the knuckles. While other rashes like a photosensitive rash (A) or a malar rash (D) can occur, they are less specific. The lesions shown in the image are characteristically seen in which type of leprosy? Such lesions are characteristic of borderline leprosy, which lies between the tuberculoid and lepromatous forms on the leprosy spectrum. Borderline leprosy demonstrates immunological instability and presents with numerous asymmetrical lesions that may vary in size and shape. The lesions are often infiltrated plaques with irregular borders and may show partial sensory loss. In contrast, lepromatous leprosy typically presents with numerous symmetrical lesions such as nodules, papules, or diffuse infiltration without well-defined margins. Borderline lepromatous leprosy tends to show more numerous and less well-defined lesions compared to borderline tuberculoid forms. Histoid leprosy is characterized by shiny, dome-shaped nodules over apparently normal skin. Thus, the annular, well-demarcated plaques seen in the image are most consistent with borderline leprosy. 183. Which of the following does not cause a rightward shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve? (A) Increased HbF (B) Raised 2,3 BPG (C) Acidosis (D) Increased EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 14. (A) Increased HbF A rightward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve signifies a decrease in hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, which facilitates oxygen unloading to the tissues. Factors that cause a right shift include increased 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (BPG) (B), acidosis (decreased pH, the Bohr effect) (C), and increased partial pressure of carbon dioxide (CO2) (D), as well as increased temperature. These conditions are typically found in metabolically active tissues. In contrast, fetal hemoglobin (HbF) (A) has a higher intrinsic affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin (HbA). This is because HbF binds 2,3-BPG less avidly. The higher oxygen affinity of HbF facilitates the transfer of oxygen from the maternal circulation across the placenta to the fetus. Therefore, an increased proportion of HbF causes a leftward shift of the dissociation curve, not a rightward shift. Which of the following does not have the presence of the sodium-iodide symporter? (A) Pituitary gland (B) Thyroid gland (C) Placenta (D) Salivary gland EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 15. (A) Pituitary gland The sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) is a membrane protein responsible for the active transport of iodide ions into cells. Its most well-known and crucial function is in the follicular cells of the thyroid gland (B), where it mediates the first step of thyroid hormone synthesis, known as iodide trapping. However, the NIS protein is also expressed in several other extrathyroidal tissues. These include the salivary glands (D), gastric mucosa, lactating mammary glands, and the placenta (C), where it plays a role in transporting iodide into saliva, milk, and to the fetus, respectively. The pituitary gland (A), however, is not known to express the sodium-iodide symporter. Its function is to regulate the thyroid gland via TSH, but it is not directly involved in iodide transport. (A) SV = End-Diastolic Volume (EDV) - End- Systolic Volume (ESV) Stroke Volume (SV) is defined as the volume of blood pumped from a ventricle of the heart during one contraction (systole). It is calculated as the difference between the volume of blood in the ventricle at the end of filling (diastole) and the volume of blood remaining in the ventricle at the end of contraction (systole). Therefore, the correct formula is SV = End-Diastolic Volume (EDV) - End-Systolic Volume (ESV). Option (C) also correctly defines stroke volume, as Cardiac Output (CO) is the product of Stroke Volume and Heart Rate (CO = SV × HR), so SV = CO / HR. However, option (A) represents the fundamental definition of stroke volume based on ventricular volumes. Option (B) and (D) are incorrect formulas. answer.explanation: retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) A 56-year-old patient with obstructive jaundice, distended gallbladder (Courvoisier sign), dilated common bile duct (CBD), and enlarged intrahepatic biliary radicles suggests distal biliary obstruction, commonly due to periampullary carcinoma, pancreatic head carcinoma, or choledocholithiasis. After ultrasound confirms obstruction, ERCP is the most useful next diagnostic test because it directly visualizes the biliary and pancreatic ducts using contrast injection via endoscopy. It accurately identifies the level and cause of obstruction, such as stones, strictures, or tumors. Importantly, ERCP is both diagnostic and therapeutic—it allows for biopsy, brush cytology, stone extraction, and stent placement to relieve obstruction. MRI (specifically MRCP) is non-invasive and useful but does not allow intervention. Endoscopic ultrasound is helpful for detecting pancreatic lesions but is not the primary ductal study. Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography is typically reserved when ERCP is not feasible. Thus, ERCP is the most useful investigation for identifying and managing the underlying cause of obstructive jaundice. What type of MRI image is shown in the provided image? options.text: Inversion recovery image AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (B) Susceptibility weighted image The provided axial MRI of the brain shows multiple small, punctate, dark (hypointense) foci scattered throughout the white matter. These represent chronic micro hemorrhages. The MRI sequence that is most sensitive for detecting blood products (hemosiderin), calcification, and iron deposition is the Susceptibility Weighted Image (SWI). SWI is a type of high-resolution 3D gradient-echo sequence that is specifically designed to be exquisitely sensitive to substances that distort the local magnetic field, a property known as magnetic susceptibility. Blood breakdown products like hemosiderin are paramagnetic and create significant signal loss on SWI, making them appear as prominent black dots. While a standard gradient echo (GRE) image (C) is also sensitive to blood, SWI incorporates both magnitude and phase information, making it even more sensitive for detecting these microbleeds. 195. From which level does the nerve supply for the indicated structure in the provided image originate? (A) Red nucleus (B) Subthalamic nucleus (C) Decussation of pyramidal tract (D) Olivary nucleus AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (A) Red nucleus 1. Identify the Structure : The image is an axial CT scan of the orbits. The arrows are pointing to the medial rectus muscles, which are responsible for adducting the eye (turning it inward). 2. Determine the Nerve Supply : The medial rectus muscle is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (Cranial Nerve III). 3. Locate the Nerve's Origin : The oculomotor nerve (CN III) originates from the oculomotor nucleus, which is located in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus. 4. Evaluate the Options : We need to find which of the listed structures is at the same level of the brainstem as the oculomotor nucleus. (A) Red nucleus : This is a major nucleus located in the tegmentum of the midbrain, at the same level as the superior colliculus and the oculomotor nucleus. Therefore, the nerve supply originates from this level. (B) Subthalamic nucleus : This is part of the basal ganglia, located in the diencephalon, superior to the midbrain. (C) Decussation of pyramidal tract : This occurs at the very bottom of the medulla oblongata. (D) Olivary nucleus : This is a prominent structure in the medulla oblongata. Therefore, the nerve supply for the medial rectus muscle originates from the midbrain, which is at the anatomical level of the red nucleus. 196. Which imaging technique is most suitable for diagnosing primary hyperparathyroidism in a woman presenting with confusion, constipation, headache, and elevated serum calcium (13.1 mg/ dL) along with elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels? (A) MRI (B) FDG PET (C) CT (D) Sestamibi Scan AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (D) Sestamibi Scan The patient's symptoms and laboratory findings (hypercalcemia with elevated ALP) are highly suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism, which is most commonly caused by a single, benign parathyroid adenoma. The goal of preoperative imaging is to localize this adenoma. The most common and effective functional imaging technique for this purpose is a Technetium-99m Sestamibi Parathyroid Scan. Sestamibi is a radiotracer that is taken up by both the thyroid gland and any hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue (like an adenoma). In a dual-phase scan, an early image shows uptake in both tissues. A delayed image (at 2-4 hours) is then taken. The tracer washes out of the normal thyroid tissue much faster than it does from the hyperactive parathyroid adenoma, which retains the tracer and appears as a persistent "hot spot." This allows for the precise localization of the adenoma before surgery. 197. Which of the following statements is accurate concerning the COVID-19 Reporting and Data System (CORADS)? (A) CORADS-0 indicates normal lung (B) CORADS-5 is typical of COVID-19 (C) Pleural thickening is typical of COVID-19 (D) Lobar consolidation is typical of COVID-19 AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (B) CORADS-5 is typical of COVID-19 The CO-RADS (COVID-19 Reporting and Data System) is a standardized scheme for reporting chest CT findings in patients with suspected COVID-19 infection. It categorizes the level of suspicion on a scale from 1 to 5. 1. CO-RADS 5 is assigned when the CT findings are typical and highly characteristic of COVID-19 pneumonia. These classic findings include bilateral, peripheral, and basal predominant ground-glass opacities, often with a rounded morphology. 2. CO-RADS 0 (A) is for an uninterpretable scan. CO-RADS 1 indicates a normal or non-infectious finding. 3. question.text: Which of the following statements is accurate concerning the COVID-19 Reporting and Data System (CORADS)?

options.label: C
options.text: Pleural thickening is typical of COVID-19

options.label: D
options.text: Lobar consolidation is typical of COVID-19 AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (B) CORADS-5 is typical of COVID-19 The CO-RADS (COVID-19 Reporting and Data System) is a standardized scheme for reporting chest CT findings in patients with suspected COVID-19 infection. It categorizes the level of suspicion on a scale from 1 to 5. 1. CO-RADS 5 is assigned when the CT findings are typical and highly characteristic of COVID-19 pneumonia. These classic findings include bilateral, peripheral, and basal predominant ground-glass opacities, often with a rounded morphology. 2. CO-RADS 0 (A) is for an uninterpretable scan. CO-RADS 1 indicates a normal or non-infectious finding. 3. Pleural thickening (C) and large lobar consolidation (D) are considered atypical features for COVID-19 and would more likely be classified as CO-RADS 3 (equivocal) or CO-RADS 4 (suspicious but not classic). 198. Which phase of the cell cycle displays the highest resistance to radiation? (A) M phase (B) G1 phase (C) S phase (D) G2 phase AAns  EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 (C) S phase The sensitivity of a cell to the damaging effects of ionizing radiation varies significantly throughout the cell cycle. Cells are most sensitive to radiation during the M (mitosis) phase and the G2 phase. They are less sensitive during the G1 phase. The phase of the cell cycle where cells are the most resistant to radiation is the late S (synthesis) phase. During the S phase, the cell is actively replicating its DNA. The presence of homologous DNA sister chromatids and the upregulation of DNA repair enzymes (like those involved in homologous recombination) during this phase are thought to confer a higher capacity to repair radiation-induced DNA double-strand breaks, thus making the cell more radioresistant. This principle is important in radiation oncology, as it influences the effectiveness of fractionated radiotherapy schedules. 199. (A) Arterial puncture (B) Thrombophlebitis (C) Empyema (D) Chylothorax Downloaded from www.pdf.tube MEDINK INICET Examination Paper (A) Posterior nucleus (B) Reticular nucleus (C) Anterior nucleus (D) Ventral lateral nucleus EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 5. (C) Anterior nucleus The structure indicated in the sagittal brain image corresponds to the mammillary body, which is part of the limbic system and lies on the inferior surface of the hypothalamus. Mammillary body sends efferent fibers via the mammillothalamic tract (bundle of Vicq d’Azyr) to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus. Anterior nucleus of thalamus receives these fibers and is an important relay in the Papez circuit, which is involved in memory and emotional processing. The pathway is: Hippocampus → Mammillary body → Mammillothalamic tract → Anterior nucleus of thalamus → Cingulate gyrus. Other options are incorrect because: 1. The posterior nucleus is involved mainly in sensory integration. 2. The reticular nucleus modulates thalamic activity. 3. The ventral lateral nucleus is primarily a motor relay nucleus. Thus, the terminating fibers from the indicated structure reach the anterior nucleus of the thalamus. In the infraclavicular fossa, which portion of this bone can be felt by touch? (A) 1 (B) 2 (C) 3 (D) 4 EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 6. (A) 1 The image displays a lateral view of the scapula with several parts labeled. Structure 1 is the coracoid process, a hook-like projection from the superior border of the scapula. Structure 2 is the acromion, 3 is the glenoid fossa, and 4 is the inferior angle. The infraclavicular fossa is the depression located immediately inferior to the clavicle. The bony structure that can be palpated deep within this fossa, medial to the head of the humerus, is the tip of the coracoid process. It serves as an important landmark and an attachment site for several muscles and ligaments. The acromion (2) is palpated at the superior-most point of the shoulder. The glenoid (3) is an articular surface and is not palpable, and the inferior angle (4) is palpated on the posterior aspect of the thorax. If a patient has low blood oxygen (hypoxemia) but a normal alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient, what medical condition does this typically point to? (A) Right to left shunt (B) Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch (C) Hypoventilation (D) Alveolar membrane damage EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 7. (C) Hypoventilation The Alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient is the difference between the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli (P O A 2) and in the arterial blood (P O a 2). It reflects the efficiency of oxygen transfer across the lungs. An elevated A-a gradient signifies a problem with gas exchange, such as a shunt (A), V/Q mismatch (B), or diffusion impairment (alveolar membrane damage, D). However, if a patient is hypoxemic (low P O a 2) but the A-a gradient is normal, it implies that the lungs are transferring oxygen efficiently. This situation arises when the hypoxemia is caused by a low partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli (P O A 2) to begin with. The two main causes for a low P O A 2with a normal A-a gradient are breathing air with a low oxygen concentration (e.g., high altitude) or hypoventilation. Hypoventilation (reduced breathing) causes an increase in arterial CO2, which displaces oxygen in the alveoli, lowering P O A 2 and consequently P O a 2. What is a characteristic feature observed in physiological jaundice? (A) Increased indirect bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine (B) Increased direct bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine (C) Increased indirect bilirubin, absent urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine (D) Increased direct bilirubin, absent urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 8. (A) Increased indirect bilirubin, increased urobilinogen, absent bilirubin in urine Physiological jaundice in newborns is a common, transient condition caused by the immaturity of the liver's bilirubin-conjugating system (low UGT enzyme activity), coupled with an increased bilirubin load from the breakdown of fetal red blood cells. This leads to an increase in unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin in the bloodstream. Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and bound to albumin, so it cannot be filtered by the kidneys, resulting in absent bilirubin in the urine. The bilirubin that is successfully conjugated and excreted into the gut gets converted by bacteria to urobilinogen. A portion of this urobilinogen is reabsorbed and excreted in the urine, so urobilinogen is present (and may be increased due to the higher overall bilirubin turnover). This pattern contrasts with obstructive jaundice, which would feature increased direct bilirubin and bilirubin in the urine. Which of the following is not associated with renal auto-regulation? (A) Tubuloglomerular feedback (B) Myogenic reflex (C) Renin-angiotensin system (D) Renal sympathetic system fibers EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 9. (D) Renal sympathetic system fibers Renal autoregulation refers to the intrinsic mechanisms within the kidney that maintain a stable renal blood flow (RBF) and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) despite fluctuations in systemic blood pressure. Superior gluteal artery 2. Inferior gluteal artery 3. Superior vesical artery 4. Middle rectal artery 5. Inferior vesical artery 6. Vaginal artery (A) 1,2,3,5 (B) 2,3,4,6 (C) 2,3,4,5,6 (D) 1,4,5,6 EXAMINATION PAPER NOV-2021 1. (C) 2,3,4,5,6 The internal iliac artery bifurcates into an anterior and a posterior division. The posterior division supplies the pelvic wall and gluteal region, giving off the iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries (1). All the other arteries listed are branches of the anterior division, which primarily supplies the pelvic viscera, perineum, and medial thigh. These visceral and parietal branches include the umbilical artery (from which the superior vesical artery (3) arises), obturator artery, inferior vesical artery (5) (in males), uterine artery (from which the vaginal artery (6) arises in females), middle rectal artery (4), internal pudendal artery, and the inferior gluteal artery (2). answer.explanation: The image points to the clavicle. The placement of a central venous catheter via the subclavian approach involves inserting a needle just inferior to the clavicle to access the subclavian vein. The subclavian artery lies immediately posterior and superior to the subclavian vein. Due to this close proximity, the most common immediate mechanical complication during a subclavian line insertion is the inadvertent puncture of the subclavian artery. This can be recognized by the pulsatile backflow of bright red blood and can lead to significant complications like hematoma, hemothorax, or pseudoaneurysm. While other complications like pneumothorax are also common, arterial puncture is generally cited as the most frequent. Thrombophlebitis (B) is a later complication. Empyema (C) is an infectious complication. Chylothorax (D) is a rare complication caused by injury to the thoracic duct, more common on the left side.
